https://www.politico.eu/article/volodymy.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy is gambling that taking the fight deeper into Russia will put enough pressure on Vladimir Putin to force him to get serious about peace talks. For much of the war, the Russian president has been able to shield ordinary Russians from the worst of the conflict. The Ukrainian leader is now trying to break that insulation — disrupting air travel and striking refineries, factories, warehouses and other targets deep inside Russia. The logic is brutal but simple: Raise the economic and political cost of the war for Russians faster than Putin can raise the military and civilian costs for Ukrainians with his escalating air assaults. Advertisement Advertisement With that aim in mind, Ukraine mounted in August one of its heaviest waves of strikes on Russia since the war started more than four years ago. The campaign expanded quickly to target not just conventional military facilities but also oil refineries, factories, and the vast warehouses of Russia’s online retail behemoths, Wildberries and Ozon. And ordinary Russians have expressed frustration at the domestic fuel shortages, the disruption of air travel and the upending of Russian e-commerce. Ukraine has scaled up domestic production of its attack drones as it tries to make the war unsustainable for Moscow. But there is little evidence yet that the disruption poses any serious threat to Putin’s hold on power. Coups have been forecast before. European spymasters, Ukrainian officials and Russian exiles have issued numerous predictions that Putin’s days are numbered, that Russians will turn on him or he’ll be ousted in a Kremlin uprising by oligarchs and Russia’s elite. Nonetheless, Putin has endured. What Ukraine’s air campaign does appear to have done is make the war harder for ordinary Russians to ignore. That’s significant given how the Kremlin has succeeded largely in silencing public dissent and has Russian-based media on a tight leash. “I don’t think the authorities’ approval rating can fail to decline when people go outside and see a huge column of smoke rising over the city, or when they arrive to a gas station and there’s no fuel, while on television they’re being told that Russia is a great oil power,” said Ian Matveev, a Russian political analyst and an associate of the late Russian dissident Alexei Navalny. Advertisement Advertisement Matveev added that Zelenskyy’s air campaign has exposed how the Russian military can’t fully protect the country. That was underscored in May when the Kremlin reluctantly pared back the Victory Day jamboree celebrating the Red Army’s defeat of Nazi Germany. Shortly after, in June, Ukraine repeatedly struck Russian oil refineries and fuel infrastructure, including around Moscow. In July, Ukrainian drones reached the Omsk refinery in Siberia, Russia’s largest, about 2,700 kilometers from Ukrainian-controlled territory, reportedly using an upgraded drone. Russia’s President Vladimir Putin arrives to attend the pared-back Victory Day military parade at Red Square in Moscow on May 9, 2026. | Alexander Kazakov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images By then, Ukrainian strikes had hit many of Russia’s major refineries, oil terminals and fuel-storage facilities. At the same time, Ukraine launched an operation against Russia’s so-called shadow fleet in the Black and Azov seas, targeting more than 200 vessels, according to Ukrainian officials. The Russian media has reported on the impact of the strikes at Wildberries and Ozon warehouses on small businesses, with sellers of clothing and electronics lamenting that they’ve lost years of work, even their livelihoods. Pro-war military bloggers have not held back on their criticism, faulting the Russian armed forces for ineffectiveness. But are these complaints enough to alarm Putin and prompt him to stop the war? Advertisement Advertisement The strikes are clearly embarrassing the Russian autocrat, said John Lough, a former NATO official who is now at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre, a think tank founded by exiled Russian businessman and prominent opposition figure Mikhail Khodorkovsky. “These attacks are damaging for Putin — more in terms of his credibility with the elites than with the population at large,” Lough said. “They can see increasingly that the war is not winnable on the terms advertised and that he has damaged rather than improved Russia’s security.” Lough said he doesn’t see a revolution or coup around the corner. “But if the fuel problems continue and more warehouses burn down, there will be more questions from the population about how long this is all going to last and why it started in the first place,” he added. To ramp up the pressure, Zelenskyy and his tacticians are now eager to make Russia’s commercial airspace increasingly difficult to use. “Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” the Ukrainian leader said last week. He warned foreign airlines to stay clear as the skies over Russia would become increasingly unsafe because of Ukraine’s drone operations. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he added. Tim Willasey-Wilsey, a former British diplomat, described Ukraine’s air campaign as “ very, very successful.” But Ukraine’s position as it enters into another wartime winter is more desperate than Russia’s, he feared. Advertisement Advertisement “I think Kyiv is terrified about going into another winter, and this time without any means to defend itself against ramped up Russia’s ballistic missile attacks,” he said. Putin is unlikely to have missed that vulnerability. Nor have Ukraine’s allies. During a meeting with Zelenskyy and top security officials from Britain, Germany and France last week, much of the focus was not on the peace deal recently proposed by a U.S. delegation fresh from a visit to Moscow. It was, according to a senior Ukrainian official who spoke to the AP, on “how to get through the winter.”

https://www.politico.eu/article/natos-pl.text: NATO’s top commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich on Monday vowed to block, blunt and break any Russian attack as part of a new “Theory of Victory,” and underlined that alliance troops would fight even if U.S. forces were engaged elsewhere. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Grynkewich outlined how the 32-member alliance would respond to an invasion of NATO territory as concerns grow that Russia could be capable of attacking a NATO member by the end of the decade . “Our alliance exists to preserve peace,” he said, “but let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then, if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.” Advertisement Advertisement The rare intervention by the four-star general to discuss a military blueprint underscores NATO’s effort to deter Russia. It is also aimed at sending a message of NATO unity after a grueling year for the alliance, which was rocked by Donald Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and infighting over the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran . Under the three-part blueprint, NATO would initially use land-based troops — buttressed by air, naval, cyber and space capabilities — to stop an assault, targeting attacking forces and preventing them from seizing territory, Grynkewich said. NATO would then use sensors and autonomous systems among other capabilities to “overwhelm enemy formations … and their advance,” he said, before using “highly effective precision munitions” and unmanned systems if necessary to “break the [enemy] warfighting system” and “everything that supports” it. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the theory laid out by Grynkewich “will send a strong message to our adversaries that we are going to defend ourselves.” NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe said he does “not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable.” But “we will … ensure any attack against any ally proves utterly futile.” The speech describes a more forceful response if a foe attacks, but its credibility depends on allies having the forces, infrastructure, and coordination to implement the plan. Advertisement Advertisement Asked whether the plan factored in a scenario where the U.S. was engaged elsewhere, Grynkewich said: “It absolutely does account for that, and in fact, it must.” Under Trump, the U.S. has sought to refocus its military on other priorities such as the Indo-Pacific, homeland security and the Western Hemisphere. U.S. ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said in Warsaw on Monday that Europe only ranks fourth among Washington’s strategic concerns. The Pentagon has already cut its contributions to NATO crisis forces and is set to unveil a review of U.S. forces in Europe by the end of the year. “No one should question the commitment of the United States to this alliance,” Grynkewich argued, but added that “ultimately, it's a political decision about who's providing troops where.” Camille Grand, NATO's former assistant secretary-general for defense investment, said the plan was “a very deliberate effort” to signal that the alliance would be ready to fight with or without large-scale involvement of U.S. forces. “For my country, fighting with Russians is with or without Americans,” said a separate senior European defense official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “We expect them to come, but if they won’t, we will fight anyway.” Advertisement Advertisement Grand added that the blueprint is also an indication that NATO is ready to take a bolder approach toward Moscow by threatening the destruction of its war machine even deep behind the front lines. That comes as Moscow sent a letter to NATO last month threatening to use its nuclear arsenal if the alliance tried to isolate its Kaliningrad exclave. Grynkewich warned that NATO would be ready to respond — even with its nuclear arsenal. “Should an adversary threaten escalation by saber-rattling, or should one actually decide to escalate during conflict, it will not fracture our alliance,” he said. “We should take comfort in our ability to deliver mass effects and the implicit warning that we could match any enemy move up the escalation ladder.”
